dz.headline: Dollar reaches 248 dinars on Algeria’s parallel market
dz.dek: The rate at Algiers’ Port-Saïd exchange square matched the dollar’s record, while the euro held at 276 dinars.
paragraphs: The US dollar traded at 248 dinars on Algeria’s parallel currency market on Saturday 21 November, matching its record against the dinar. The rate at Port-Saïd square in Algiers, the country’s main parallel exchange market, was two dinars below the 250-dinar threshold.

The dollar was quoted at 24 800 dinars per 100 dollars, a new record, after trading at 247.5 dinars on Tuesday and 245.5 dinars on 9 November, TSA Algerie reported. The euro remained at 276 dinars, unchanged from 10 days earlier.
On the official market, the dollar rose to 136.96 dinars on Friday 20 November, while the euro edged down to 150.43 dinars. The dollar’s official high was 147.17 dinars, set on 7 February 2022.

dz.headline: Algerian army breaks up drug network and arrests 17
dz.dek: Army security services seized 19 quintals of processed cannabis from Morocco, along with vehicles, motorcycles and 273 million centimes.
paragraphs: Algerian army security services dismantled a drug-trafficking network during the week and arrested 17 people, the Defence Ministry said Saturday 21 November. The network was trying to bring 19 quintals of processed cannabis from Morocco into Algeria, the ministry said.

The operation also seized 50 utility vehicles, five motorcycles, a jet ski, mobile phones and 273 million centimes, according to the ministry. It said the security services acted in the army’s 2nd Military Region, but did not identify the arrested people or say what legal steps they would face.

Separately, Algerian border guards shot dead two Moroccan drug traffickers in the Naâma region on Friday after they refused to stop while attempting to bring more than 50 kilograms of cannabis into Algeria, the ministry said.

dz.headline: Algeria seeks diaspora help to reach 8 million tourists by 2029
dz.dek: Tourism Minister Houria Medahi urged Algerians abroad to invest, share expertise and promote the country as the government targets more visitors.
paragraphs: Algeria is asking its diaspora to help develop tourism as the country targets 8 million visitors by 2029. Tourism Minister Houria Medahi and Sofiane Chaib, the secretary of state responsible for Algerians abroad, chaired a meeting with diaspora business operators, investors, tourism professionals and startup representatives on Thursday.

Medahi outlined investment opportunities in hotels and other accommodation, desert and mountain tourism, wellness, leisure facilities, tourist transport and digital services, according to a Tourism Ministry statement. She said diaspora involvement should extend beyond financing to transferring expertise, modernising management, building international partnerships and attracting tour operators.
The minister also called for promotion of Algeria as a destination in foreign markets and for local products and crafts to be included in tourism routes.

dz.headline: Algerian physicist says tensions drove his move from France to the US
dz.dek: Noureddine Melikechi says he left for the United States after fearing the social climate in France would not suit his family.
paragraphs: Noureddine Melikechi, an Algerian physicist who later worked at the United States National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), says he left France for the United States after deciding the social climate was unsafe for raising his children. He told his story in a biography written by Rym Khelil. Melikechi had studied in Algeria and the United Kingdom before taking academic posts in France.

Melikechi passed the lecturer competition in 1994 and became a university professor the following year. He joined the University of Toulouse in summer 1996, where he said he learned from a research team and worked with advanced equipment. But he recalled continuing tensions between Algeria and France, and said Algerian colleagues in French universities were also considering moves to the United States. Some told him they felt they were not treated like French-born colleagues despite their qualifications and professional skills.

Melikechi recalled that a childhood friend with a new doctorate in computer science was considering leaving France in 1995 amid the far right's electoral rise. The University of Massachusetts recently named one of its research programmes after Melikechi, and President Abdelmadjid Tebboune congratulated him.

ao.headline: Rui Verde says China-linked reconstruction left Angola with debt and misused funds
ao.dek: The author’s new book traces more than two decades of ties built through private deals, Chinese companies and public money.
paragraphs: Rui Verde’s new book says Angola’s postwar partnership with China brought reconstruction loans and Chinese companies, but also diverted funds and debt the country is still paying. The book examines more than two decades of relations after the civil war ended in 2002.

In an interview with Lusa, Verde said the relationship was conducted through individuals rather than states. He identified businessman Sam Pa, his partner Lu Fong, former Sonangol chairman Manuel Vicente and former state minister Manuel Hélder Vieira Dias “Kopelipa” among the central figures. Verde said funds were diverted, many through state oil company Sonangol, and loans were poorly applied.

The network came under greater scrutiny after José Eduardo dos Santos left power in 2017 and João Lourenço became president, Verde said. His book is titled “Redefining the China-Angola Relationship: Privatization, Development and Disenchantment.”

bj.headline: Burkina Faso records 580 Beninese among returnees from Guinea
bj.dek: The government says talks with the relevant embassies are under way to organise the return of people expelled from Guinea’s gold-mining sites.
paragraphs: Burkina Faso recorded 580 Beninese among people received at a transit centre in Bobo-Dioulasso after Guinea expelled gold miners. The Burkinabe government announced the figure on Friday 20 November 2026, as it said its repatriation operations had ended.

The centre took in 1 994 foreign nationals from 11 countries, according to the Burkinabe government’s information service. Togo accounted for 983 people, followed by Benin, Ivory Coast with 150 and Niger with 133. The service said discussions with the countries’ embassies were under way to arrange their return.

The last convoy from Guinea arrived during the night of 18 to 19 November. Burkina Faso then ended reception and registration at Bobo-Dioulasso and Koloko; regional emergency-relief councils remain available for any remaining cases.

bj.headline: Abomey-Calavi mayor urges residents to stay clear of roadworks and reservoirs
bj.dek: Mayor Nathanaël D. Koty has published safety rules for the construction of rainwater reservoirs and nearby road projects.
paragraphs: Abomey-Calavi's municipality has urged residents living near construction sites to take extra care while work continues. In a statement released on Saturday, 21 November, Mayor Nathanaël D. Koty set out safety rules for the building of reservoirs designed to hold rainwater.

Residents must stay within marked zones and never cross a barrier, even to shorten a journey. Parents were told to keep children away from the reservoirs, and swimming, fishing, taking water or dumping waste in them is banned. Anyone who falls into a basin should call emergency services with the exact location and alert a site worker, without attempting a rescue in the water.

Broken barriers or suspicious activity can be reported to a site worker, on free number 7011, or to the site health, safety and environment team at 01 52 77 56 15, 01 67 95 46 90 or 01 59 93 27 12. The works include the Djonou bridge at Godomey and the widening of the Missessinto–Allada road to 2×2 lanes.

bj.headline: Benin’s foreign minister presents investment and AI priorities in Oslo
bj.dek: Corinne Amori Brunet urged alliances with local businesses and backed regulated artificial intelligence at a meeting of African and Nordic foreign ministers.
paragraphs: Benin’s foreign minister, Corinne Amori Brunet, presented the country’s governance record and economic priorities at a meeting of African and Nordic foreign ministers in Oslo, Norway, on 19-20 November. She urged alliances with local actors to attract investors and argued for artificial intelligence governed in the service of development.

At a trade and investment round table, Brunet highlighted small businesses’ role in creating jobs. Benin’s eligibility score for the Open Government Partnership rose from 10 to 12 out of 16 between 2022 and 2024, with progress in open budgeting. A 2022 International Monetary Fund assessment also cited progress on internal controls and audit, and the establishment of a Court of Accounts was under way.
Brunet moderated an artificial-intelligence session attended by more than 15 delegations. African and Nordic countries committed to encouraging responsible use of the technology.

bj.headline: China gives Benin army CFA20 million in farm equipment
bj.dek: The machines are destined for women's village groups and cooperatives, with delivery to the field scheduled for the week of 7 December.
paragraphs: China has donated agricultural equipment valued at CFA20 million to Benin's armed forces for distribution to women's village groups and cooperatives. Chinese Ambassador Zhang Wei and Brigadier General Abdoul-Baki Sanni Bachabi, the defence minister's chief of staff, signed the documents formalising the handover. Benin's public broadcaster, the Benin Radio and Television Office (SRTB), announced it on 21 November.

The equipment is intended for villages including Segbana, where it includes rice hullers, a shea-nut crusher and an oil press, and Karimama, where a motorised tiller with a trailer is planned. The army's director for participation in development and public-interest tasks said the equipment would be provided free, with training in operation and maintenance and spare parts for breakdowns.
Transport to the villages is scheduled for the week of 7 December. The donation falls under the army's civil-military activities.

bj.headline: Benin's media regulator pledges training support to four outlets
bj.dek: Stations in Tchaourou, Savè and Dassa-Zoumè were also reminded to follow the broadcasting terms they accepted.
paragraphs: Benin's High Authority for Audiovisual and Communication (HAAC) said it would keep helping media outlets with training after visits to four stations in the Borgou and Collines departments on Friday, 20 November 2026. Media professionals in the two regions asked for stronger training during the sixth day of the regulator's national tour.

The delegation visited Tchaourou FM, Idadu FM in Savè, La Voix des enfants of SOS Children's Village and Soha TV, both in Dassa-Zoumè. HAAC president Édouard Loko reminded the radio and television stations to respect the specifications they had committed to, and talks covered their facilities, broadcast hours and programmes.
The training requests followed similar appeals from three northern stations on 19 November during the tour's fifth day. The national tour was due to continue on Saturday, 21 November.

bw.headline: Botswana lawmakers question Moti’s citizenship as projects lack firm terms
bw.dek: The government says Zunaid Moti was security-vetted before President Duma Boko granted citizenship under existing presidential powers.
paragraphs: Botswana lawmakers are scrutinising the citizenship granted to South African businessman Zunaid Moti, whose proposed investments include a manufacturing plant in Gabane expected to employ about 1,200 people. President Duma Boko used discretionary powers under Section 10 of the Citizenship Act to register him as a citizen.

Higher Education Minister Prince Maele told Parliament that Moti had undergone security checks. The government has linked his arrival to the plant, a proposed five-star hotel near Gaborone Dam and a pledge to build 100 schools. The plant would make prefabricated components for public infrastructure; Boko said about 73% of its materials would come from Botswana.

Tswapong South MP Kesitegile Gobotswang questioned how Moti qualified before the investor-focused citizenship framework was fully operational. Parliament passed the Citizenship (Amendment) Act in December 2025, but project timelines, investment values and whether commitments are legally binding remain unanswered.

bf.headline: Burkina Faso reports 956 cybercrime victims and CFA261 million in losses
bf.dek: Mobile Money fraud accounted for 263 victims and more than CFA104 million stolen, while online shopping scams caused nearly CFA57 million in losses.
paragraphs: Cybercrime affected 956 people in Burkina Faso in October 2026, causing estimated financial losses of more than CFA261 million, according to figures published by the security ministry's communications directorate and the Central Brigade for the Fight Against Cybercrime. Authorities recorded 615 information and communications technology fraud cases, the most frequent offences.

Mobile Money scams accounted for 263 victims and more than CFA104 million stolen. Online shopping fraud affected 240 people, with losses estimated at nearly CFA57 million. The figures also included 51 cases of webcam blackmail and 72 cases of illegal account access. In October, authorities arrested 21 people, 15 of whom were referred to justice, the ministry's programme Réflexe sécurité reported.

The authorities advised people to check sellers before paying, keep passwords private and preserve transaction records. Victims of webcam blackmail were urged not to pay, to secure their accounts and to alert the relevant services.

bf.headline: Yambressinga urges Burkina Faso to replace municipal special delegations with revolutio...
bf.dek: The governance specialist says the appointed bodies have put routine administration ahead of investment and local development in the communes.
paragraphs: Guilga François de Paule Yambressinga, a doctor of economic and social history and a specialist in territorial governance, has called for the special delegations running Burkina Faso's municipalities to be replaced by municipal revolutionary councils. In an opinion article published on Lefaso.net, he argues for reform of local government across the country.

Yambressinga says all Burkinabe communes have been administered by special delegations since 2022. He argues the bodies tend to favour the management of day-to-day affairs over structural investment and local development initiatives, and says their functioning does not match a decree dated 16 March 2026.

He also argues that the Popular Progressive Revolution should be reflected in how local authorities are governed. The article is an argument by an individual and reports no government decision on the proposal.

bf.headline: Burkina Faso’s security minister calls for joint operations and intelligence sharing
bf.dek: Mahamadou Sana says security forces must pool resources and plan operations together while retaining their separate identities.
paragraphs: Burkina Faso’s Security Minister Mahamadou Sana called for the country’s internal security forces to share resources and intelligence and coordinate operations at a ministry council meeting in Ouagadougou on Friday, 20 November. The session focused on improving cooperation among the forces.

Sana said threats including terrorism, cross-border crime, cybercrime and everyday insecurity required a collective response. Pooling resources would not merge the forces or erase their identities, he said; it would involve sharing information and planning operations together. The ministry said national strategies for internal security, road safety and the protection of mining sites were finalised and awaiting adoption.

The ministry is implementing national strategies against drugs and cybercrime and has begun drafting an action plan against corruption and related offences. Sana also cited forest security measures and the redeployment of the national police and gendarmerie among actions taken in 2026.

bf.headline: Burkina Faso trains 99 retiring military personnel in farming and livestock
bf.dek: The graduates studied crop production and animal husbandry and pledged to start projects at a small scale before expanding them.
paragraphs: Burkina Faso’s defence ministry closed its 18th agriculture and livestock training session for military personnel preparing to leave service on Friday, 20 November, in Ouagadougou. 99 participants completed the 2026 course, which combined classroom lessons, practical work and field visits.

Pale Soyo Ardiouma, representing the trainees, said the lessons covered soils, crop selection and cultivation, livestock management, animal health and processing animal products. He said graduates had committed to drawing up business plans suited to their regions, resources and skills, then applying the techniques on a small scale before expanding.

The trainees recommended that military personnel begin retraining five years before retirement. They also called for a ministry unit to equip and support former military and paramilitary personnel pursuing agriculture and livestock projects.

bf.headline: CFPEM-SST backs Burkina United Fight League’s second edition
bf.dek: The combat-sports event pairs fighters from Burkina Faso and Nigeria in Ouagadougou under the theme “Le Réveil Patriotique.”
paragraphs: The Centre for Professional Training in Mining Equipment and Occupational Health and Safety (CFPEM-SST) says it will support the second Burkina United Fight League (BUFL), a combat-sports competition scheduled for 22 November 2026 in Ouagadougou. The event is set for the Salle des banquets de Ouaga 2000.

The league says fighters from Burkina Faso and Nigeria will compete, with American trainer Dewey Cooper also taking part. The centre was invited by Burkinabè athlete Iron Biby and says its backing is intended to support sporting talent and youth development.
The edition, titled “Le Réveil Patriotique,” is due to begin at 19 h. Organisers say they want to strengthen Burkina Faso’s place in international sports competitions.

bi.headline: Rwasa files independent bid for Burundi’s 2027 presidency
bi.dek: The former National Congress for Liberty leader paid a 100 million-franc deposit and says he cannot obtain a required party-membership certificate.
paragraphs: Agathon Rwasa, a former leader of Burundi’s National Congress for Liberty (CNL) and a longtime opposition figure, filed an independent candidacy for the presidency on Saturday, 21 November. The election is scheduled for 3 May 2027. He submitted his papers to the national electoral commission after paying a deposit of 100 million Burundian francs to the central bank on 20 November.

The commission requires independent candidates to provide proof that they belong to no political party. Rwasa said he cannot obtain that certificate under current circumstances. He said his departure from the CNL leadership was an expulsion, not a voluntary resignation, and argued that this makes him eligible to run independently.
Francis Rohero, president of the FP Ineza party, also filed a candidacy, while Aloys Kamenyero submitted an application missing several documents, SOS Medias Burundi reported.

bi.headline: Burundi educator presses for Braille access and school exams for blind pupils
bi.dek: Jean-Marie-Vianney Zingiza says abbreviated Braille would make books received from abroad usable and help blind students keep pace in class.
paragraphs: Jean-Marie-Vianney Zingiza, a former teacher and Braille educator in Burundi, is advocating for blind pupils to have accessible books, trained teachers and the chance to continue to university. He says many books received from abroad use abbreviated Braille, which many Burundian teachers and pupils cannot read.

Abbreviated Braille uses shorter signs for words or groups of letters than full Braille, taking less space and allowing faster reading and note-taking with practice. Zingiza says pupils writing letter by letter can fall behind as a teacher dictates. He returned to teaching in 2008 at the Rumuri Centre, after losing his sight in 1991.

From 2008 to 2012, blind pupils were not allowed to take the national examination at the end of sixth year, according to the account. After Zingiza pressed for access, the education minister authorised six pupils to sit it in 2012; two passed.

bi.headline: Burundi researcher explains how earthworms turn waste into compost
bi.dek: Eric Kazitsa says vermicomposting uses farm and food-processing residues, while well-raised worms can produce more than 20 offspring a month.
paragraphs: Eric Kazitsa, a researcher and lecturer in natural sciences at Burundi’s Higher Teacher Training College, says vermicomposting uses earthworms and microorganisms to break down organic matter into compost. The process has three stages: pre-composting, active decomposition and maturation.

Kazitsa says agricultural and agro-processing residues can serve as the material, which is dried to raise its carbon content; cow dung can be added to increase nitrogen. Earthworms prefer acidity levels between 6 and 8, so acidic waste such as citrus should be avoided or treated to neutralise it. As worms consume and digest the material, they produce castings that mature into a stable, nutrient-rich compost ready for use.
Kazitsa says a worm can lay eggs two or three times a week. When raised well, it can produce more than 20 individuals by the end of a month.

cm.headline: Cameroon's deposits fund gives Afriland eight days to pay CFA141.96 billion
cm.dek: The demand covers principal, interest and penalties tied to a dispute involving MTN Cameroon and companies linked to businessman Baba Ahmadou Danpullo.
paragraphs: Cameroon's Deposits and Consignments Fund (CDEC) has given Afriland First Bank eight days from receipt of its November 18 demand to transfer CFA141.96 billion tied to a dispute involving companies linked to businessman Baba Ahmadou Danpullo and MTN Cameroon. CDEC Director General Richard Evina Obam warned the bank that compulsory debt recovery proceedings would follow if it misses the deadline.

The demand comprises CFA126.63 billion in principal and CFA15.33 billion in interest and penalties. The funds relate to precautionary seizures in September 2022 on accounts associated with MTN Cameroon and Mobile Money Corporation, among others, sought by Danpullo-linked companies operating as Bestinver.

The Douala-Bonanjo Court of First Instance ordered Afriland in November 2023 to set aside CFA126,629,176,833 immediately, with a CFA50 million daily penalty for delay. The CDEC demand concerns the bank's handling of funds subject to that order.

cm.headline: Golar LNG books CFA3.23 billion in Cameroon exit costs
cm.dek: The gas company took the charges after its Perenco contract expired and its floating gas vessel sailed out of the country.
paragraphs: Golar LNG has booked $5.4 million, about CFA3.23 billion, in employee termination costs after its Hilli Episeyo floating liquefied natural gas facility stopped operating in Cameroon. The charges show up in the company's financial statements for the first nine months of 2026, published on November 18.

In the segment results, Golar said Cameroonian labour law governed the charges, which followed the expiry of its contract with Perenco and the vessel's departure. It declined to say how many workers were hit or how much had already been paid out. The total climbed from $2.5 million at March 31 to $4.8 million at June 30 and $5.4 million at September 30.
The third-quarter addition of $600,000 was up 12.5% on the June total. The disclosures do not show how much cash has actually gone to departing staff.

cm.headline: Cameroon’s CAA fails twice to shortlist Green Climate Fund legal consultant
cm.dek: The public institution’s latest recruitment ended unsuccessfully, leaving it without a candidate for the legal opinion required in its accreditation preparations.
paragraphs: Cameroon’s Autonomous Sinking Fund (CAA) has failed for a second time in three months to shortlist a consultant for a legal opinion needed in its preparations for Green Climate Fund accreditation. The public institution declared the latest recruitment unsuccessful in a notice signed on November 13 and published four days later by the Public Procurement Regulatory Agency.

The CAA’s previous attempt produced the same result on August 14. Its latest call for expressions of interest, issued on September 21, covered two assignments: an institutional integrity policy and complaints mechanism, and an external opinion on whether the fund has the capacity to act as an accredited entity.
The legal review was intended to assess the CAA’s administrative and financial autonomy. The institution remains without a selected candidate for that assignment.

cm.headline: Sofitoul convenes Cameroon tourism forum on private investment
cm.dek: The Yaoundé meeting will examine regulatory, administrative and financial barriers to tourism projects and possible incentives for investors.
paragraphs: Travel services company Sofitoul is hosting a forum on public-private partnerships at the Hilton Hotel in Yaoundé on November 20–21, seeking ways to attract private investment to Cameroon's tourism infrastructure. The event is part of the company's 20th anniversary celebrations.

A press kit released on November 14 says government officials, project finance specialists and tourism professionals will discuss regulatory, administrative and financial obstacles to tourism projects. The forum is expected to be chaired by the Minister of Tourism and Leisure.

Participants will consider tax incentives, public guarantees and joint financing by government and private operators. They will also review financing approaches used in other countries for possible adaptation to Cameroon.

cf.headline: Central African Republic cabinet grants Green Mining two industrial mining permits
cf.dek: The permits were approved at the cabinet meeting of 23 July 2026, the latest in a run of concessions that the report says are handed out to private groups.
paragraphs: The Central African Republic's cabinet validated two industrial small-mine exploitation permits for the company Green Mining at its meeting on Thursday, 23 July 2026, according to Corbeau News Centrafrique.

The report says the permits are part of a long list of concessions distributed to private groups, with investors and business networks lining up in Bangui. It gives no locations, minerals or investment values, and it reports no financial returns to the population.

cf.headline: Adouma accuses Central African Republic president of nepotism
cf.dek: The opposition figure says family favoritism shapes senior appointments and blames the president for entrenched administrative failures.
paragraphs: Raymond Adouma, an opposition figure, accused the Central African Republic’s president of fostering nepotism and political favoritism in public appointments during an interview on Radio Ndeke Luka. He said the practices contradicted official promises to reform government and had weakened the administration.

The report says 72% of the previous ministerial team was retained. It also says four ministers missed the first cabinet meeting of the president’s seven-year term. Adouma’s allegations come as three quarters of citizens are reported to live below the poverty line, on less than CFA1,000 a day.

The report also alleges that more than 100 mining permits went to foreign operators, while royalties account for four per cent of state budget revenue. It says residents in eastern provinces face poisoned waterways and the loss of fishing activity.

cf.headline: Central African authorities face questions over route to dissolve state body
cf.dek: Corbeau News Centrafrique questions whether the handling of a possible dissolution reflects legal uncertainty or the use of law for political ends.
paragraphs: A Corbeau News Centrafrique article asks whether the Central African authorities’ handling of a possible dissolution of the BRDC reflects legal uncertainty or the use of law for political ends. The article frames the choice as one between an administrative process and a judicial one, and does not report that either route has been completed.

The article opens with a definition of the rule of law: an order based on the law in force, public freedoms, and procedural and judicial guarantees. It does not identify a formal decision, a court action or a timetable for the body’s dissolution.
The article’s stated concern is whether the authorities’ approach is legally uncertain or politically motivated.

cf.headline: Paris colloquium outlines legal routes to pursue Wagner crimes
cf.dek: The March 2 gathering focused on crimes by Wagner and affiliates, including individual prosecutions and universal jurisdiction in third countries.
paragraphs: A March 2 international colloquium at the Sorbonne in Paris examined legal responsibility for crimes attributed to Russia’s Wagner group and its affiliates, with a focus on victims in the Central African Republic. Organised by the Sorbonne’s Institute for Research in International and European Law with partner organisations, the gathering brought together investigators, lawyers, academics and human-rights advocates.

Participants outlined three avenues: individual prosecutions for war crimes, crimes against humanity and serious violations of international humanitarian law; use of universal jurisdiction by third countries; and stronger investigations before the International Criminal Court. The report identified regions including Lobaye, Nana-Mambéré and Ouham-Pendé among those whose residents were affected.

The colloquium also considered Wagner’s changing names, opaque contracts and uncertain status as a private military company or an arm of the Russian state. The report did not identify any prosecution or court action launched at the event.

km.headline: Comoros opens renovated lycée with library and science rooms

paragraphs: Comorian President Azali Assoumani inaugurated a renovated lycée in Fomboni, on the island of Mohéli, on Saturday, 21 November. The school now bears the name of Mohamed Hassanaly, a Mohéli politician who took part in negotiations over Comoros’ independence.

Students have a library, a computer room, science classrooms and a laboratory, as well as work areas and adapted toilets. Assoumani thanked France and the French Development Agency for supporting the Comoros Emerging Plan and their work in education.

Hassanaly was a deputy for Mohéli and agriculture minister, and served as vice-president when Comoros gained sovereignty in 1975. He also took part in the steps that led to the country’s admission to the United Nations that year.

cg.headline: MaishaPay launches merchant payment and stock platform in Congo
cg.dek: The service links sales tracking and mobile-money or card payments with Linkia, which lets wholesalers and retailers order stock and pay suppliers.
paragraphs: MaishaPay, an African fintech company, began operating in Brazzaville on 21 November with a payment terminal and Linkia, a platform connecting merchants and suppliers. Founder Landry Ngoya Kasim said the service is designed to help merchants manage sales and stock.

The terminal accepts Mobile Money and card payments, depending on which services are activated, while Linkia lets wholesalers order stock and pay for goods from their shops or sales points. A Vival corporate sales manager said the platform centralises transactions and allows the wholesaler to collect recorded payments at the end of the day. Merchant Jolie Moly said she has used MaishaPay for three months and can pay suppliers electronically or in cash; customers can pay through Mobile Money or Airtel Money and receive invoices tracking their purchases.
Founded in the Democratic Republic of Congo in 2018, MaishaPay also operates in Ethiopia, Nigeria and Côte d’Ivoire.

ci.headline: West African ministers weigh host for new central bank
ci.dek: At a November 20 meeting in Abidjan, finance ministers also examined the regional payment system, a solidarity fund and a transition framework.
paragraphs: Ministers responsible for the planned West African currency met in Abidjan on November 20 to decide where the future regional central bank will be based. The meeting was the sixth session of the presidential task force on the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) currency, known as the ECO, which is due to start gradually in 2027.

Ivory Coast's Economy, Finance and Budget Minister, Adama Coulibaly, opened the talks on behalf of President Alassane Ouattara and urged member states to make concrete proposals to clear remaining institutional and political blockages. Ministers were also due to consider the regional payment and settlement system, a Solidarity and Stabilisation Fund, governance rules and a transition framework, based on a technical committee report prepared in Abidjan from November 17 to 19.

The launch was first targeted for 2020, but was postponed after the Covid-19 pandemic and failures to meet convergence criteria. A roadmap adopted in June 2021 set 2027 as the new deadline, and the minister said respect for macroeconomic convergence criteria remains the condition for the currency's credibility.

ci.headline: CAF raises annual payments to 54 member associations to 700 000 dollars
ci.dek: The increase follows a 31,2 million dollar net profit and a recovery from 16,8 million dollars in reserve deficits to a 14,4 million dollar surplus.
paragraphs: The Confederation of African Football (CAF) raised its annual allocation to each of its 54 member associations to 700 000 dollars from 200 000 dollars in 2021. The increase took effect in July 2026, according to financial statements presented Saturday in Abuja, Nigeria.

CAF reported a net profit of 31,2 million dollars for the financial year ending in June 2026, with revenue of 284 million dollars, up more than 200 %. Its reserves moved from a deficit of 16,8 million dollars to a positive balance of 14,4 million dollars, and cash stood at 118,8 million dollars. CAF said the allocations are intended to strengthen administration, youth football and women’s football.

The six regional unions’ allocation rose from 500 000 to 900 000 dollars. Investment in clubs increased from 19 to 48 million dollars, while the prize for the winner of the CAF Champions League rose to six million dollars from 2,5 million dollars in 2021.

ci.headline: PI Holding creates PI Auto Services after buying Fix N’Go’s mechanical business
ci.dek: The new POINT S-branded subsidiary will handle vehicle servicing and repairs, while Fix N’Go is expected to support a transfer of expertise.
paragraphs: PI Holding launched PI Auto Services in Abidjan on Friday 20 November 2026, after signing an agreement to buy the mechanical-work business operated by Fix N’Go. The new subsidiary will provide vehicle maintenance and repairs under the POINT S brand, including mechanical work, oil changes, tyres, bodywork and paint.

Sébastien Kadio-Morokro, Petro Ivoire’s chief executive and a PI Holding leader, said Fix N’Go would help transfer expertise to the new company. PI Auto Services takes over an activity Petro Ivoire and Fix N’Go had developed under the POINT S name since 2020. Kadio-Morokro said the group wanted the subsidiary to become a reference for vehicle maintenance in Ivory Coast in the medium term and across Africa in the long term.

Petro Ivoire deputy managing director Maud Kadio-Morokro said the fuel distributor’s products had grown by about 21% through the end of September 2026, three times faster than the market. She also said Petro Ivoire operates half of the national electric-vehicle charging network.

eg.headline: Egypt signs deal to restart about 100 idle oil wells
eg.dek: The state petroleum corporation and Weatherford will use AI to assess wells nationwide and pick interventions that need no drilling rigs.
paragraphs: Egypt's state petroleum corporation, the Egyptian General Petroleum Corporation (EGPC), and Weatherford, a global company, signed a framework agreement on Friday to bring about 100 idle oil wells back into production over the next 18 months. The programme covers onshore and offshore areas nationwide. Petroleum Minister Karim Badawy witnessed the signing.

Badawy said AI systems will analyse data from the idle wells, assess whether production can resume and identify the most suitable technology for each well. The interventions can be carried out without drilling rigs, which saves time and costs, the ministry said.

Badawy said the programme supports the ministry's five-year plan to raise oil and gas output through the end of the 2029/2030 fiscal year. It complements ongoing exploration, prospecting and field development. The ministry is also working with specialised international companies on the transfer of expertise.

eg.headline: Egypt offers foreign visitors visa and medical-travel support
eg.dek: A tourism expert says the measures cover entry, accommodation and transport, with help for international patients and their companions.
paragraphs: Egypt has introduced measures to simplify visits by foreigners, including streamlined visa applications and easier booking, accommodation and transport, tourism expert Mohamed Abdel-Dayem said. The support is intended to cover the journey from a visitor’s home country through departure from Egypt, with particular attention to medical patients and tourists.

Abdel-Dayem, a member of the General Assembly of the Chamber of Tourism Companies, said patients and companions can get help with visas, travel arrangements, airport reception and transport. eg.headline: Cairo court to hear lawyer's trial over alleged leak in school assault case
eg.dek: The lawyer represents several child victims from Seeds Language School, where 12 defendants were sentenced to six months in prison for endangering children.
paragraphs: On Saturday the Cairo Misdemeanor Appeals Court in First Settlement is due to take up the case against a lawyer for several child victims of sexual assault at Seeds Language School, who is accused of leaking sensitive details of the investigation.

Earlier, the New Cairo Misdemeanor Court handed 12 defendants six months in prison, a bail of 5,000 Egyptian pounds and a matching fine over the endangerment of children at the school. The charges followed negligence that let several students be sexually assaulted on school premises.

Investigators found children were left without adequate supervision in the schoolyard and while waiting for buses. The Public Prosecution relied on surveillance footage, testimony from Education Ministry officials and a report on the victims' psychological state.

gq.headline: Equatorial Guinea’s Malabo and Bata ports win regional recognition
gq.dek: The awards came at the close of a five-day regional meeting that set commitments on port modernisation, digital services and maritime cooperation.
paragraphs: The ports of Malabo and Bata received recognition for modernisation and operating capacity at the close of a regional ports meeting in Sipopo, Equatorial Guinea, on Friday. The gathering ran from 16 to 20 November and combined the 46th annual council meeting of the West and Central Africa Ports Management Association (AGPAOC) with its fourth International Blue Economy Forum.

More than 400 delegates, port officials, experts and international partners attended, according to the report. AGPAOC Secretary-General Jean-Marie Koffi presented the final Sipopo declaration, which sets out member states’ commitments on resilient and sustainable ports, digital port services, energy transition and technical cooperation on climate challenges.

Equatorial Guinea’s environment and blue economy minister, Fidel Esono Mba Eyono, said the country would focus on six priorities, including maritime governance, coastal ecosystem protection and smart infrastructure. The new AGPAOC president, Conakry Port director-general Aly Koïta, called for regional cooperation to reduce logistics barriers and improve trade connectivity.

gq.headline: Equatorial Guinea orders technical review of five proposed cultural sites
gq.dek: A South Korean architecture firm presented museum designs for three cities and cultural centres for Annobón and Ciudad de La Paz.
paragraphs: Equatorial Guinea's Vice-President Nguema Obiang Mangue has asked TAEIN Development, a South Korean architecture company, to hold technical meetings on plans for three museums and two cultural centres. The museums are proposed for Malabo, Bata and Ciudad de La Paz; the centres for Annobón and Ciudad de La Paz.

The government's State Works Monitoring Commission and GEPROYECTOS are to work with the company to adapt the designs to government requirements. Decisions remain on room capacity, exhibition layouts, collections and the conditions needed to house and preserve objects. The sites would include exhibition rooms and educational areas focused on the country's history and culture.

Separately, the Ministry of Information, Press and Culture presented an inventory of cultural objects held abroad, identifying countries and their current institutional or private custodians. The ministry said it had completed a preliminary research phase.

er.headline: U.S. lawmaker links Eritrea trade talks to progress on peace
er.dek: Representative Jim Baird's proposed Eritrea PILLAR Act would open U.S. farm exports, mining help and port access to talks once peace steps are taken.
paragraphs: Jim Baird, a Republican congressman from Indiana, is set to introduce the Eritrea PILLAR Act and the Ethiopia SPARK Act, which tie formal trade talks with the United States to steps toward lasting peace. The bills were expected to be introduced Thursday and shared with The Hill.

The texts seek to increase Eritrean and Ethiopian access to U.S. corn, soybeans, soybean meal, livestock feed, farm equipment and agricultural research. They also call for U.S. help in mining gold, silver, copper, zinc, iron ore, potash and other minerals, access to port infrastructure, and reduced tariffs or better trade terms. Baird said the plan would make the United States a preferred partner over China, which has deep ties in both countries.

The proposal comes as Ethiopian and Eritrean forces build up along their shared border, Reuters reported, and after fighting broke out in September between Ethiopia's federal government and rebels in Tigray. Secretary of State Marco Rubio spoke with Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed Ali on October 14 and called for a return to the 2018 Ethiopia-Eritrea peace framework.

ke.headline: Murkomen opens police hiring to observers at 423 centres
ke.dek: Kenya’s nationwide constable recruitment is scheduled for December 10, with applicants required to arrive by 8am.
paragraphs: Kenya’s Interior Cabinet Secretary Kipchumba Murkomen said independent observers will be allowed at recruitment centres for the nationwide police constable exercise scheduled for December 10. The National Police Service plans to hold the exercise from 8am to 5pm at 423 centres across all 47 counties.

Murkomen said observers would help ensure that qualified candidates are selected without corruption or interference. Applicants must be Kenyan citizens aged 18 to 28, hold national identity cards and have at least a D+ in the Kenya Certificate of Secondary Education, including in English or Kiswahili. The service said recruitment is free and warned that paying bribes or seeking to influence selection are criminal offences.

Candidates must bring identity cards, birth certificates, academic certificates and testimonials. The service also requires applicants to meet physical and medical fitness standards, including minimum heights of five feet eight inches for men and five feet three inches for women.

ke.headline: Heifer assessment targets year-round feed supply for Kenya’s dairy farmers
ke.dek: The study finds costly, seasonal feed and uneven services constrain productivity, while Kenya produces 5.2 billion to 5.76 billion litres of milk a year.
paragraphs: Heifer International Kenya’s Dairy Value Chain Gap Analysis identified feed supply, farm services and market efficiency as constraints on the country’s dairy sector. Findings were presented at a media roundtable in Nairobi on November 19, as Kenya pursues higher productivity under its National Agri-food Systems Investment Plan for 2026–2030.

Across 11 counties, the study held 54 engagements, with detailed assessments in Nyandarua, Embu and Elgeyo Marakwet. Smallholders in Nyandarua get three to 15 litres per cow each day, against 25 to 30 litres on intensive farms. Farmers face high feed costs, seasonal shortages, inconsistent quality and limited mechanisation and conservation services, and the assessment calls for businesses able to supply quality feed throughout the year.

Kenya produces 5.2 billion to 5.76 billion litres of milk annually, against domestic demand of 12.76 billion litres. The investment plan estimates an annual feed gap of 30 million tonnes, based on 2021 figures. Ainabkoi Dairy Cooperative Society chairman Luke Kesei said unpredictable milk prices make it difficult for farmers to plan investments.

ke.headline: Ledama defends shooting threat over KSh365,000 employment claim
ke.dek: The Narok senator says alleged auctioneers entered a company linked to him and took the keys to its delivery truck under a court order.
paragraphs: Narok Senator Ledama Olekina defended a threat to shoot men filmed in a confrontation near a vehicle, saying alleged auctioneers had entered private company premises and taken the keys to its delivery truck. He said they were seeking KSh365,000 over a former Senate employee’s compensation claim, and denied that his personal vehicle was being auctioned.

In a statement on Saturday, November 21, Olekina said the dispute stemmed from a staff member dismissed in 2017 and a Labour Court order authorising property attachment. The former employee, Zakayo Rotiken, worked as a Narok North Constituency Coordinator from 2017 to 2020; the Employment and Labour Relations Court ruled in his favour on October 31, 2023, over his dismissal and unpaid salary arrears.

Olekina said Senate employment obligations are funded through the Parliamentary Service Commission, not individual senators, and accused political opponents and social media platforms of misrepresenting the video. He questioned the legal basis for attaching assets of a separate private company.

ke.headline: Diaspora group urges Sifuna to fund JKIA expansion without foreign investors
ke.dek: At a New Jersey meeting, a Kenyan in Ohio said overseas Kenyans could pool money and partner with the government to modernise the airport.
paragraphs: Kenyans living in the United States have urged Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna to seek diaspora funding for the expansion of Jomo Kenyatta International Airport (JKIA), rather than bring in foreign investors. The proposal was presented on Saturday at a meeting with Sifuna and other Linda Mwananchi supporters in New Jersey.

Kiemo Mohando, a Kenyan based in Columbus, Ohio, said Kenyans abroad could combine contributions and work with the government on the airport. He pointed to billions of shillings sent to Kenya annually and called for a coordinated funding arrangement, including ways for diaspora members to contribute directly to development institutions. No funding target or commitment was announced.

The proposal follows the government’s 2024 plan to give India’s Adani Airport Holdings a 30-year concession for a project estimated at $1.85 billion. The plan included a second runway and a new passenger terminal; aviation workers and two Kenyan organisations challenged the arrangement.

za.headline: ANC seeks city power-sharing deals by 27 November
za.dek: The party won 31% of the vote but the most votes in just two of South Africa’s eight cities.
paragraphs: Parties in South Africa have until 27 November to negotiate and form local governments, and the African National Congress (ANC) is seeking power-sharing agreements to run cities after its losses in this month’s local elections.

Its share of the vote fell to 31%, from 46% in the last local election, and it won the most votes in only two of the country’s eight cities, against six in 2021. The ANC took a majority in just Limpopo, one of South Africa’s nine provinces, down from six provinces previously.

In Gauteng, home to Johannesburg and Pretoria, the pro-business Democratic Alliance took the most votes in both cities and in Ekurhuleni, the province’s other main region. The ANC still won more votes overall than any other party, but it lost control of more than half the councils it had held in 2021.

za.headline: First-time buyers make up 48.5% of South African home-loan applications
za.dek: Ooba data show first-time buyers averaged an 8.5% deposit, while approval rates reached 83.9% this year.
paragraphs: First-time buyers made up 48.5% of South African home-loan applications in October, according to ooba Home Loans data cited by Pam Golding Properties. Their share averaged 46.9% for the year to date.

The buyers put down an average deposit of 8.5% of the purchase price, compared with 12.8% across all homebuyers in the year to October. Effective loan approval rates averaged 83.9% this year, and ooba secured an average rate of prime minus 0.77% in October, the data showed.

Applications including legal, tax and administrative costs made up 10.1% of applications in September and October. The South African Reserve Bank left the repo rate unchanged at its November meeting, with the prime lending rate at 10.75%.

The buyers put down an average deposit of 8.5% of the purchase price, compared with 12.8% across all homebuyers in the year to October. Effective loan approval rates averaged 83.9% this year, and ooba secured an average rate of prime minus 0.77% in October, the data showed.

Applications including legal, tax and administrative costs made up 10.1% of applications in September and October. The South African Reserve Bank left the repo rate unchanged at its November meeting, with the prime lending rate at 10.75%.

za.headline: South Africa convenes committee as macadamia pest reaches 34,000 hectares
za.dek: The felted coccid affects nearly half the country’s cultivated macadamia area, with severe infestations cutting yields and putting jobs at risk.
paragraphs: South Africa’s Department of Agriculture says the macadamia felted coccid pest has spread across about 34,000 hectares of orchards, nearly half the country’s cultivated area. It was confirmed in Ohrigstad, Limpopo, in November, after spreading across Mpumalanga from its first detection in Barberton Valley in 2017.

Farm inspections found leaf damage, dying canopies and fewer nuts; some trees had more than 80% canopy damage. In a severe-spread scenario, about 14,600 hectares in Mpumalanga face yield losses of up to 70%, with 5,950 jobs at risk. Macadamias South Africa says it has spent more than R6.3 million on research through 2026. Growers report pesticide costs rising from R60,000-R70,000 per hectare without the pest to R100,000 when control is added.

After November farm visits, the government convened stakeholders to discuss an action plan. A steering committee led by national and provincial governments is proposed to coordinate research, registrations, grower support and orchard rehabilitation.

za.headline: Ramaphosa orders flags at half-mast for Mlambo-Ngcuka through 28 November
za.dek: South Africa’s first female deputy president will receive a Category 2 state funeral, with a memorial service scheduled for Tuesday in Johannesburg.
paragraphs: Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka, South Africa’s first female deputy president and a former United Nations under-secretary-general, died on Friday, 20 November, aged 71. President Cyril Ramaphosa confirmed she will receive a Category 2 state funeral.

The Presidency said the funeral will include ceremonial elements by the South African National Defence Force and take place on Saturday, 28 November, at Middledrift in the Eastern Cape. Ramaphosa ordered the national flag flown at half-mast at flag stations from Sunday morning, 22 November, until the evening of 28 November.

A state memorial service is scheduled for 14:00 on Tuesday, 24 November, at Our Lady of Lourdes Catholic Church in Rivonia, Johannesburg. Mlambo-Ngcuka had also served as minister of minerals and energy and chancellor of the University of Johannesburg.

za.headline: Springboks reach Nations Championship final despite 20-17 loss to Ireland
za.dek: Ireland beat South Africa in Dublin, but the Springboks' losing bonus point puts them through to the final at Twickenham.
paragraphs: Ireland beat South Africa 20-17 in Dublin on Saturday, but the Springboks earned a losing bonus point for losing by fewer than seven points and qualified for the Nations Championship final. The match was at the Aviva Stadium, and the defeat was the Springboks' second in a row after losing to France the previous weekend.

Ireland led 17-10 at halftime and scored three tries to South Africa's two. Ireland won the lineout ball, dominated the breakdown and kept the Springboks pinned in their own half for much of the game. Rassie Erasmus, the banned head coach, watched from the team hotel.

The final is at Twickenham next Sunday, when South Africa are due to meet either France or England. France were scheduled to play Argentina later on Saturday, and England's win over the All Blacks on the same day means they will qualify if South Africa lose.

ng.headline: Rights group sues Nigeria's data regulator and electoral commission over AI-altered vot...
ng.dek: The Socio-Economic Rights and Accountability Project seeks a court order compelling an investigation into suspected AI-generated photographs in the voters' register.
paragraphs: The Socio-Economic Rights and Accountability Project (SERAP), a rights group, has sued Nigeria's National Data Protection Commission (NDPC) and the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) at the Federal High Court in Abuja. The suit, numbered FHC/ABJ/CS/2863/2026, asks the court to compel the NDPC to decide whether to investigate suspected AI-generated photographs, altered personal data and unverifiable records in INEC's preliminary Register of Voters.

INEC said on 1 November that its Automated Biometric Identification System had flagged 268 records for review, with some individuals allegedly exploiting official registration credentials. SERAP wants the NDPC to obtain and examine INEC's records and data, and to exercise its enforcement powers under the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023, including corrective orders, fines and compensation for affected voters.
SERAP argues that the irregularities raise serious concerns about the security of Nigerians' personal data and the reliability of the register ahead of the 2027 general elections.

ng.headline: Kogi soldiers seize two AK-47s in raid on bandit enclave
ng.dek: The army says its intelligence-led operation in Okehi was aimed at kidnap gangs behind recent abductions along the Kabba–Okene Road.
paragraphs: Troops of the Nigerian Army have driven suspected armed bandits out of a hideout in Okehi Local Government Area of Kogi State, seizing two AK-47 rifles, three magazines and 65 rounds of ammunition. The operation took place on Saturday, November 21, 2026.

Acting Director of Army Public Relations Colonel Appolonia Anele said Patrol Base Kabba launched the raid with other security personnel. In the Osara, Gada and Ohakiti forest areas, soldiers met about six armed men at an abandoned settlement and forced them to flee, the army said. Bags, torchlights, food and a power bank believed to belong to the fleeing men were also recovered.

The army said the raid aimed to dismantle hideouts tied to recent kidnappings on the Kabba–Okene Road and neighbouring communities. It urged the public to keep passing timely and credible information to security agencies.

ng.headline: CAF returns to profit with $31.2 million net surplus
ng.dek: Africa's football governing body books a $31.2 million net gain on $284 million in revenue, its first profit after years of financial strain.
paragraphs: Africa's football governing body, the Confederation of African Football (CAF), has posted a net profit of $31.2 million for the financial year ended June 2026, on revenue of $284 million. The results were presented at CAF's 48th Ordinary General Assembly in Abuja on 21 November.

The figures show a return to profitability for a body that had spent years in financial difficulty, and the assembly was the setting for the presentation. CAF's leadership has credited its reforms under president Patrice Motsepe for the turnaround.
The reported figures do not include a breakdown of where the revenue came from or how the surplus will be used.

et.headline: Ethiopia's ride-hailing sector pays 340 million birr in income tax
et.dek: More than 30 platforms compete in Addis Ababa on fares and vehicle types, while 33,000 drivers, most of them self-employed, carry the costs of fuel and rent.
paragraphs: More than 30 ride-hailing platforms operate in Addis Ababa, where passengers compare fares, choose vehicle types and see the price before booking. Options range from economy cars to motorcycles for short trips. A nurse in Bahir Dar said she books a ride after her 11:00 pm shift, reaching home about 20 minutes sooner than by public bus.

Over 33,000 drivers in Addis Ababa have generated more than 340 million birr in income tax for the sector. Self-employed drivers, many of whom rent their cars, work without guaranteed earnings or social protection. A driver in Adama said fuel, maintenance and taxes take a large share of his income, leaving what remains to cover rent, school fees, food and car repayments.

In Dire Dawa, about 6,000 Bajaj make up most of the public transport network. Researchers want rural Ethiopia to promote motorcycle-based transport, and they urge the government to ease the import barriers that keep those vehicles expensive.

et.headline: Exporters warn smuggling is undermining Ethiopia’s pulses and oilseeds trade
et.dek: The exporters’ association says illegal channels are weakening formal sales as Ethiopia seeks to expand processing, quality and overseas markets.
paragraphs: The Ethiopian Pulses and Oilseeds Exporters Association warned that cross-border smuggling is undermining Ethiopia’s formal exports of pulses and oilseeds. Association President Idao Abdi said agricultural commodities continue to leave through illegal channels despite government efforts to curb the trade.

Trade and Regional Integration Minister Yasmin Wahabrebi said action against illegal trade requires coordination across government institutions. She said foreign-exchange reforms had reduced some incentives for smuggling, especially those linked to black-market currency trading. Neither speaker estimated how much product or export value was lost.

The association said Ethiopia exported 555,000 metric tonnes of pulses and oilseeds last year, earning more than US$571 million. Abdi said post-harvest losses could reach 25% of harvested crops, while exporters also need investment in processing, quality and access to markets.

et.headline: Ethiopian-born children report unequal access to citizenship
et.dek: Some children of Ethiopian mothers and foreign fathers say they struggle to secure nationality, while another man obtained an identity card and passport without difficulty.
paragraphs: Children born and raised in Ethiopia to Ethiopian mothers and foreign fathers describe sharply different paths to citizenship. Monica Marcel, born in Addis Ababa to an Ethiopian mother and a Congolese father who arrived as a refugee, said she and her siblings have struggled to obtain Ethiopian nationality and still receive services under refugee status.

Marcel said her family repeatedly sought answers from authorities about their applications. She said the lack of citizenship exposed her to discrimination at school; her child’s future also worries her. Wude Kassa, 64, said her six children with her Congolese husband have not obtained citizenship and face difficulties finding employment despite growing up and studying in Ethiopia.
Louis Bauna, 54, said he obtained citizenship without difficulty. His mother’s nationality, birth certificate and other documents enabled him to get an Ethiopian identity card and passport.

et.headline: Ethiopia’s startup law opens incentives to foreign founders
et.dek: Article 40 allows foreign startups and ecosystem builders to access incentives, while excluding foreign startups from the grant programme.
paragraphs: Ethiopia’s Startup Proclamation creates a legal framework for startups and allows foreign startups and startup ecosystem builders to access incentives under Article 40. The provision excludes foreign startups from the startup grant programme and also addresses exemption from the minimum capital requirement under the Investment Proclamation.

Capital Ethiopia’s analysis says the law could help entrepreneurs connect with investors, financial institutions, universities, research centres and government support. But it argues that legal recognition alone will not ensure jobs or viable businesses, particularly for young Ethiopians who have ideas and skills but lack finance, institutional backing and market opportunities.

The article says foreign startups could bring technology, investment, jobs and links to international markets, while questioning whether they should receive the same public support as Ethiopian startups in an economy facing youth unemployment and limited access to finance. It calls for attention to implementation and policy priorities.

gh.headline: Accra court sets GH¢100,000 bail for teacher accused of drug sales
gh.dek: Kanayo Nwachukwu must surrender his passport and report to police each Friday while Ghana's Food and Drugs Authority (FDA) examines seized products.
paragraphs: An Accra Circuit Court granted Kanayo Nwachukwu, a 49-year-old man who claimed to be a teacher, GH¢100,000 bail with two sureties over the alleged sale of unregistered drugs. The court ordered one surety to be justified and the other to earn at least GH¢2,500 a month.

Nwachukwu must deposit his passport with the court and report to the police investigator every Friday between 0700 and 1400. He cannot leave Ghana without notifying the court or investigator. Police Inspector Rebecca Ellimah said officers from the Police Headquarters' Special Operations Team arrested him during an October 9 operation at Okaishie Drug Lane and recovered 10 boxes of tapentadol 100mg, three boxes of timaking 100mg and six boxes of Royal 'Apentadol Apple 225mg. The exhibits are with the Food and Drugs Authority (FDA) for examination; his plea was not taken while the court awaits its report.
The prosecution was directed to follow up with the FDA before Nwachukwu's next court appearance, scheduled for December 21, 2026.

gh.headline: Vanderpuye proposes 1% salary fund for NDC workers’ pensions

paragraphs: Edwin Nii Lante Vanderpuye, one of four aspirants for the National Democratic Congress (NDC) chairmanship, has proposed a pension scheme for party workers at every level if elected. gh.headline: Asiedu Nketiah says Asante regalia loans fall short of restitution
gh.dek: The NDC chairman says some royal objects displayed at the Manhyia Palace Museum remain on loan from British museums rather than transferred to community ownership.
paragraphs: Johnson Asiedu Nketiah, chairman of Ghana’s National Democratic Congress (NDC), said the Asante people deserve more than temporary access to royal regalia taken during colonial military campaigns. Speaking at the Movement for Freedom of Nations Assembly in Moscow on November 16, he said objects returned for display at the Manhyia Palace Museum in Kumasi were subject to different arrangements: some had been restituted, while others remained on loan from British museums.

Asiedu Nketiah said a loan does not transfer ownership, and argued that restored rights and accepted obligations should guide assessments of redress. He said claims over identifiable objects could be investigated, while reparations for the transatlantic slave trade raised harder questions about responsibility, applicable law and who should benefit. He called for evidence-based claims and responses that can be implemented.

He also said affected communities should help design reparative agreements and scrutinise proposed remedies. He urged the assembly to support existing African Union and Caribbean reparations mechanisms rather than create parallel institutions.

gh.headline: Jospong subsidiary and Turkish firm begin Ghana farm-product trials
gh.dek: The research will test whether products made from discarded shrimp and crab shells protect crops, improve soil and offer farmers cheaper inputs.
paragraphs: Under a memorandum of understanding signed at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, the African Agribusiness Consortium (AAC), a subsidiary of Ghana’s Jospong Group of Companies, and ChitoGlobal Biotechnology will test farm products made from discarded shrimp and crab shells on Ghanaian farms. The products are based on chitosan, a substance found in crustacean shells, and the first step is joint research and field trials.

Those trials will examine whether the products protect seeds and plants, help crops withstand dry spells, strengthen natural defences against fungal disease, and affect soil quality and yields. Jospong’s Chief Investment and Innovation Officer, Noah Gyimah, said the company will first secure approval from Ghana’s environmental and standards authorities before using the products on its farms. AAC will also assess commercial viability, potential buyers and whether Ghana has enough raw material for local production.

If the trials prove the products suitable, AAC intends to make them available to smallholder farmers. The consortium also plans to test their use on its own commercial rice, maize, vegetable and soybean crops.

gh.headline: Ghana reaches first Amputee World Cup final after Turkey shootout win
gh.dek: The Black Challenge beat defending champions Turkey 4-2 on penalties and will meet Morocco in an all-African final in Mexico.
paragraphs: Ghana’s Black Challenge reached the 2026 Amputee Football World Cup final in Mexico after beating defending champions Turkey 4-2 on penalties on Saturday. The semi-final ended 1-1 after extra time, and the shootout secured Ghana’s first place in the tournament final.

The African Paralympic Committee, which oversees African Paralympic sport, congratulated Ghana and Morocco after both teams qualified. The committee said their performances also challenged perceptions of disability. The teams will meet at 1:30am Monday, each seeking its first World Cup title.

Ghana began the tournament with a 2-0 loss to Angola and a 1-1 draw with Colombia, then beat Iraq 6-0 to advance from its group. In the knockout rounds, it defeated the United States 3-0 and Egypt 2-0 before the Turkey match.

tz.headline: Tanzania study urges cheaper finance for small traders
tz.dek: A 14-month study of 350 traders found heavy reliance on cash and personal funding, alongside gaps in digital finance use.
paragraphs: A study commissioned by the Financial Sector Deepening Trust followed 350 small-scale traders in Tanzania for 14 months, recording business and household transactions to track how they earn, spend, save and use financial services. Its findings call for more affordable services, financial education and flexible financing for small businesses.

Deputy Industry and Trade Minister Denis Londo said 38% of traders used personal savings to finance their businesses, while 33% relied on relatives and friends. About 70% of transactions were in cash, although 65% of traders had bank accounts. More than 80% did not use digital transactions extensively; 40% cited cost and 31% limited experience as barriers. The study also found average profits at male-owned businesses were approximately 73% higher than at women-owned enterprises.

Londo said financial institutions should design products around traders’ circumstances. Financial Sector Deepening Trust chief executive Eric Massinda said the research tracked transactions rather than relying on traders to recall and report their activity.

tz.headline: Nyanzaga gold mine in Tanzania readies first gold pour for January 2027
tz.dek: The Sengerema project, 80% owned by Perseus Mining, has paid local suppliers and the government 457.7 billion/- in its build-up since July 2024.
paragraphs: Nyanzaga, a gold project in Sengerema District, Mwanza Region, is targeting its first gold pour in January 2027 after 17 years of exploration and construction. Sotta Mining Corporation Limited, a joint venture between Perseus Mining, which holds 80%, and the Government of Tanzania, which holds 20%, is developing the project.

Country Manager Isaac Lupokela told the Seventh Tanzania Mining and Investment Conference (TMIC 2026) in Dar es Salaam that the company is preparing to commence production. Between July 2024 and March 2026, the project contributed 457.7 billion/- directly to Tanzania, including 371.6 billion/- spent on local suppliers and 60.7 billion/- paid to the government. More than 3,600 people work at the site, including 281 direct employees, most of them Tanzanians.
Nyanzaga is expected to produce an average of more than 200,000 ounces of gold a year from the 2028 to 2035 financial years, making it Perseus Mining's fourth gold mine in Africa.

tz.headline: Tanzania calls for digital infrastructure to get equal priority in Africa
tz.dek: Communications Minister Angellah Jasmine Mbelwa Kairuki made the case at an investment dialogue in Singapore, where financing and public-private partnerships were also discussed.
paragraphs: Tanzania's Communications and Information Technology Minister, Angellah Jasmine Mbelwa Kairuki, asked that digital infrastructure be given the same priority as conventional projects in Africa's development agenda. Speaking at the Africa-Singapore Infrastructure Investment Dialogue in Singapore, she said information and communication technologies are now essential to energy, electricity grids, ports and transport.

Kairuki said stronger partnerships between African and Asian governments and private firms could attract investment and speed up infrastructure building. Singapore's Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development, Alvin Tan, pledged his country's cooperation with Africa in infrastructure, energy, transport, the digital economy, fintech and cross-border payments.

Tan also said talks are continuing on a Free Trade Agreement between Singapore and the East African Community, which Tanzania belongs to. The dialogue explored innovative financing and public-private partnerships, and Invest Africa's chief executive, Chantelé Carrington, said further cooperation is expected in 2027, when Singapore chairs ASEAN.

ma.headline: Spain sends Morocco 170 files to return unaccompanied minors from Ceuta
ma.dek: Spanish police say the families of the children have been identified and have agreed to their return, but Rabat has not responded to any of the files.
paragraphs: Spanish police have submitted 170 case files to Moroccan authorities seeking the return of unaccompanied Moroccan minors in Ceuta so they can rejoin their families. The files were sent through Spanish consulates in recent months after officers identified the families and obtained their consent.

Citing police sources, the Spanish outlet The Objective reported that Moroccan authorities had not responded to any of the files despite repeated follow-ups. It also said Spain's Ministry of Children and Youth had taken over the handling of the files, a claim a ministry spokesperson denied, saying the police commissariat remains responsible under Spanish regulations.

Spanish authorities had sent 189 files to Moroccan diplomatic missions as of Tuesday, including 19 reportedly forwarded by the ministry. Ceuta is hosting about 3,767 migrant minors in 23 reception centres, while about 500 others were reportedly sleeping on the streets.

ma.headline: FIFA to inspect six Moroccan cities for 2030 World Cup preparations
ma.dek: The delegation will assess sports infrastructure, transport networks and accommodation capacity as Morocco prepares to co-host the tournament with Spain and Portugal.
paragraphs: A FIFA delegation is due to begin inspecting six Moroccan cities on 28 November as part of preparations for the 2030 World Cup, which Morocco will co-host with Spain and Portugal. The tour will cover Rabat, Casablanca, Tangier, Marrakech, Agadir and Fez.

The international football federation’s delegation will assess the progress of sports infrastructure, transport networks and accommodation capacity. A separate report says its technical team will examine stadiums, transport and hotel capacity in the six cities being considered to host matches.
Morocco plans to propose the future Grand Stade Hassan II as the venue for the final. FIFA’s inspection tour in Morocco is scheduled to follow visits to Portugal and Spain.

ma.headline: Morocco wins four places on CAF committees, including a chairmanship
ma.dek: CAF approved the appointments at its assembly in Abuja, while Fouzi Lekjaa left the finance committee and kept his first vice-president role.
paragraphs: Morocco secured four positions on the Confederation of African Football’s (CAF) restructured standing committees at the body’s assembly in Abuja, Nigeria, on Saturday, November 21. Taha Mansouri was named chairman of the Futsal and Beach Soccer Development Committee, while Abdellatif Moktarid joined the Club Competitions Committee.

Former Moroccan footballer and coach Fathi Jamal was appointed to the Technical Development Committee, and Ezzedine Yacoubi joined the Youth Competitions Committee. CAF approved the appointments as it renewed eight standing committees. Fouzi Lekjaa left the finance committee but retained his position as CAF’s first vice-president.

The youth committee oversees tournaments for under-17, under-20 and under-23 players. The club committee handles continental tournaments and related organization, while the technical committee works on training and football development across African federations.

ma.headline: Morocco meets Ghana in Amputee Football World Cup final
ma.dek: Morocco reached its first final by beating Brazil 2-1, overturning a one-goal deficit in a match decided late in the tournament.
paragraphs: Morocco will play Ghana in the 2026 Amputee Football World Cup final on Sunday, November 22, at San Martín Stadium in San Juan de los Lagos, Mexico. Both countries are seeking their first world title in the competition. The match kicks off at 7:30 p.m. local time, which is 2:30 a.m. Moroccan time on Monday, November 23.

Morocco reached the final after beating Brazil 2-1 on Friday, its sixth consecutive win in the tournament. Ghana advanced after a 1-1 draw with defending champions Türkiye and a 4-3 penalty shootout victory. The World Amputee Football Federation's official YouTube channel will show the final live and free of charge.

The two sides last met in the 2024 African Amputee Football Cup of Nations final in Egypt, which Ghana won 2-1. Morocco's previous best World Cup finish was fifth place in 2022. The 2026 tournament features 24 national teams from four continents, playing across four venues in Mexico.

ma.headline: Moulay Rachid presides over Marrakech festival opening dinner
ma.dek: The prince, who leads the festival foundation, joined a dinner hosted by King Mohammed VI as the 23rd edition began.
paragraphs: Prince Moulay Rachid, president of the Marrakech International Film Festival Foundation, presided over a royal dinner at El Badi Palace in Marrakech on Saturday, marking the official opening of the festival’s 23rd edition. Princess Lalla Oumkeltoum accompanied him at the event hosted by King Mohammed VI.

The festival’s nine-member competition jury will assess 14 feature films for the Étoile d’Or, its highest award. Oscar-winning French actress Marion Cotillard chairs the jury, which includes Moroccan filmmaker Saïd Hamich Benlarbi and Tunisian director Kaouther Ben Hania. The selection focuses mainly on first and second feature films.
The festival, which opened Friday evening at the Palais des Congrès, runs through November 28, with screenings, tributes, filmmaker conversations and professional development programmes.

ug.headline: Uganda signs 10-year crude marketing deal with Vitol
ug.dek: The trader will sell Pearl Sweet crude to international buyers and train the state oil company as exports are expected in early 2027.
paragraphs: Uganda signed a 10-year agreement with international energy trader Vitol on Friday, November 20, allowing the company to market the country’s Pearl Sweet crude to international buyers. President Yoweri Museveni witnessed the signing at State House in Entebbe, alongside officials from the Uganda National Oil Company (UNOC) and the energy ministry.

Vitol will provide UNOC with technical guidance, training and access to buyers as the state company builds its own crude-marketing capacity. Energy Minister Monica Musenero said commercial arrangements and market readiness had to be in place before production could lead to international sales.

Under the initial terms, Uganda will sell crude on a Free on Board basis at the export terminal in Tanga, Tanzania, where the East African Crude Oil Pipeline ends; buyers will arrange transport from there. The government will later assess whether to extend the deal to cover transport to final destinations. Exports were expected to start in early 2027.

ug.headline: Uganda sets 500,000-tonne cocoa target for 2036
ug.dek: The 10-year strategy also targets US$3 billion in annual export earnings and higher domestic processing.
paragraphs: Uganda has launched a 10-year cocoa strategy targeting annual production of 500,000 metric tonnes by 2036, up from approximately 72,000 tonnes. The plan also targets annual export earnings of US$3 billion and aims to raise domestic processing from less than five per cent to 30% of national output.

The Ministry of Agriculture, Animal Industry and Fisheries launched the strategy, developed with support from the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, Enabel and industry stakeholders. More than 100,000 farming households are supported by the industry. The plan targets average farm productivity of 1,000 kilogrammes per hectare, compared with 530 kilogrammes, and at least 45% participation by women and young people in the value chain.

Cocoa export earnings rose from $70.6 million in the 2015/2016 financial year to US$620.4 million in 2024/2025, according to ministry and Bank of Uganda figures. Implementation is intended to address low productivity, limited processing and access to finance, as well as climate risks and traceability requirements.
