sn.headline: Senegalese young reporters convene African media conference in Dakar
sn.dek: The 23-24 November gathering will examine how news organisations can fund journalism while preserving editorial independence.
paragraphs: The Convention of Young Reporters of Senegal (CJRS) and the Konrad Adenauer Foundation will hold the Conference of Young African Journalists in Dakar on 23 and 24 November 2026. Media professionals from across Africa are due to discuss economic models that can sustain independent journalism.

The organisers say the agenda will address financial difficulties facing press companies, digital transformation, falling advertising revenue, changing news consumption and the arrival of new players. Participants will consider how media organisations can secure durable, diverse funding while protecting editorial independence, credibility and their role in democratic life.

The organisers also plan networking and exchanges of practices and experience among young journalists. They say the conference will explore cooperation and possible initiatives for a more resilient media sector.

sn.headline: Dakar health university puts counterfeit drugs and AI on 23 November agenda
sn.dek: The University of Health Sciences of Dakar will convene an international scientific day on medical training, patient safety and medicine quality.
paragraphs: The University of Health Sciences of Dakar (USSD) will hold an international scientific day on 23 November to examine changes in medical training and health care, as it marks 10 years since its founding. The event will address artificial intelligence, telemedicine, patient safety and falsified medicines.

Three round tables will cover the governance of medical technologies, the One Health approach and substandard or counterfeit medicines. The university said discussions on medicine quality will include quality control, market surveillance and securing pharmaceutical supply chains. Speakers will also share experiences from Dakar’s Dalal Jamm and Principal hospitals and the health emergency operations centre, including responses to Rift Valley fever.

The opening lecture by Professor Serigne Maguéye Guèye will address challenges and prospects for health sciences training in Africa. USSD, founded in 2016, says it plans to expand its courses, digital teaching and research in the next decade.

sn.headline: Senegal sends music delegation to Rabat to pursue export markets
sn.dek: About 30 music professionals attended Visa For Music, where Senegalese acts performed and representatives explored links with foreign industry players.
paragraphs: Senegal sent an official delegation of about 30 music-industry professionals to Visa For Music, held in Rabat, Morocco, from 18 to 21 November 2026. The 13th edition brought together artists, producers, managers, touring agents and cultural promoters focused on music from Africa and around the world.

The delegation’s participation was backed by the Fund for the Development of Urban Cultures and Creative Industries (FDCUIC) and the Agency for the Development and Supervision of Small and Medium Enterprises (ADEPME). During the four-day event, members took part in showcases and performances, while seeking links with foreign professionals and routes to international markets for Senegalese productions.

The two Senegalese bodies said they intend to support cultural talent and businesses in expanding internationally. Discussions at the event also examined how cultural events can generate economic activity and support local economies.

sl.headline: Sierra Leone regulator reports NLE 7.4 million in 2024 revenue
sl.dek: The Sierra Leone Electricity and Water Regulatory Commission said levies and licences brought in the income, up from NLE 2.3 million in 2023.
paragraphs: The Sierra Leone Electricity and Water Regulatory Commission (SLEWRC), which licenses and regulates electricity and water providers, recorded internal revenue of NLE 7.4 million in 2024, up from NLE 2.3 million in 2023. The money came from levies and licences.

Deputy Director Sama Sandi told a Ministry of Finance budget discussion on 21 August 2024 that the commission had been allocated NLE 954 thousand for recurrent spending in the 2023 financial year but received nothing from the ministry. The commission said it resolved an average of 80% of complaints within a week and took enforcement action against 64 non-compliant water companies.
For 2024, the commission was allocated NLE 911 thousand in recurrent spending and again received none, Sandi said. He submitted a budget of NLE 5,590.29 for the 2025 to 2027 period.

sl.headline: Sierra Leone charcoal trade sustains families as tree loss threatens land
sl.dek: A government energy compact says only 15% of the population has access to clean cooking, while charcoal production removes trees.
paragraphs: Pa Alimamy, a 65-year-old charcoal burner in Sierra Leone, has worked in the trade for more than two decades and says it supports his family. Charcoal is widely used in Freetown and other regional headquarters towns, where households rely on it for cooking.

The government’s National Energy Compact, developed with World Bank support, says 36% of the population has access to electricity and 15% to clean cooking. Paul Lamin, the Environmental Protection Agency’s director of natural resource governance, said burners are cutting economic trees, including orange and mango, leaving land bare and threatening food security.

Lamin said trees take a long time to regrow, and acknowledged that people have limited alternative energy options. A Food and Agriculture Organization report estimates traditional wood energy emits 1/2.4 GT of carbon dioxide equivalent annually, or 2-7% of human-caused greenhouse gas emissions.

sl.headline: Sierra Leone civil society group demands finance minister's dismissal
sl.dek: The Consortium on Public Accountability says hardship reflects poor inflation control and reckless borrowing, which a rebuttal disputes.
paragraphs: The CSOs Consortium on Public Accountability has called for the immediate dismissal of Sierra Leone's Finance Minister, Sheku Ahmed Fantamadi Bangura. In a response published by Politico SL, writer Foday M. Daboh argues the demand confuses economic hardship with policy failure.

Daboh says Sierra Leone avoided default, stayed engaged with an International Monetary Fund programme and retained access to concessional financing under Bangura. He cites central bank statements and IMF reports as showing inflation declined after fiscal and monetary tightening, and says debt remains at high risk of distress but is mainly concessional, with commercial borrowing restrained.

The consortium's statement, as described by Daboh, alleges poor inflation control and reckless debt accumulation. He says the country has no Eurobond exposure or hidden debt; the response does not include the consortium's full case.

sl.headline: Five Sierra Leone agribusinesses advance US$64 million financing pipeline
sl.dek: The firms met institutional financiers at the inaugural West African Integration and Investment Summit in Lungi; deals still require approvals and contracts.
paragraphs: Five Sierra Leonean agribusinesses are advancing toward closing US$64 million in financing after matchmaking sessions at the inaugural West African Integration and Investment Summit in Lungi. The five were among nine West African businesses whose combined investment pipeline totals US$261 million, according to an update from the Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security.

The Sierra Leonean firms include Fambul Rice, operations at the Tormabum rice platform, Continental Food Action and Aquatic Centre, Jman Fisheries, Falcon Trading and Muloma. They met institutional financiers Oakwood Green Africa and Bloom Bank during the summit’s Deal Room sessions. Agriculture and Food Security Minister Henry Musa Kpaka said the government’s Feed Salone programme had de-risked investment, and that the ministry had encouraged banks to expand agricultural lending by linking them with local businesses.
Kpaka said the focus now moves to due diligence, board approvals and contract signings before the regional pipeline can enter implementation and create jobs.

sl.headline: Sierra Leone and TİKA discuss youth innovation centre in Mile 91
sl.dek: The proposed centre would offer young people skills, technology, entrepreneurship and leadership training, alongside talks on agribusiness projects.
paragraphs: Sierra Leone's Youth Affairs Minister Ibrahim Sannoh met Abdullah Eren, president of the Turkish Cooperation and Coordination Agency (TİKA), at its headquarters in Ankara, Türkiye, to discuss expanding work on youth skills, agribusiness and innovation.

The central proposal is to establish Sierra Leone's first National Youth Innovation and Transformation Centre in Mile 91. The planned hub would provide skills development, technology, entrepreneurship and leadership training for young people. Sannoh also discussed new joint initiatives, including agribusiness projects led by young people.

The Sierra Leone delegation included James B. Sandi, director of programmes at the Ministry of Youth Affairs, and Engineer Mohamed Sallieu Bah, secretary-general of the Foundation of Turkish Graduates.

so.headline: Somalia's opposition rejects president's offer of election talks
so.dek: The leaders turned down a meeting at the president's proposal, saying the election model must be reversed before any engagement, while the Constitutional Court has ordered.
paragraphs: Somalia's opposition leaders rejected President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's latest offer of talks after he asked former Prime Minister Abdi Farah Shirdon to host a meeting at his home. Mohamud promised major concessions and said the country's future and upcoming elections should be settled by broad consensus.

Shirdon relayed the offer, which opposition leaders debated on Thursday night and rejected when they reconvened on Friday. They say Mohamud must first abandon his one-person, one-vote election model and agree that election rules be decided by all political stakeholders. Their other conditions include international mediation, guarantees of good-faith negotiations, and security assurances for regional leaders, including the president of Puntland.

The Constitutional Court recently declared Mohamud's term extension null and void, ruled that he is unlawfully in office and ordered elections within 90 days. It also required a political agreement within 30 days. Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Egypt have joined Western and East African partners in urging an electoral agreement.

ss.headline: Magwi access roads ease farmers’ route from fields to markets
ss.dek: Residents say a community road linking farming areas to the main route is helping vehicles carry produce without getting stuck.
paragraphs: Rehabilitated access roads in parts of Magwi County, Eastern Equatoria State, are making it easier for farmers to move produce from their fields to markets, residents say. A community road connects farming areas to the main route, while work on the Magwi-Palotaka feeder road is ongoing.

Olaraga Simon Ogenga, a 35-year-old farmer, said vehicles had previously become stuck when carrying produce from farms. Aloyo Josephine, a 32-year-old farmer and mother of four, said the road had improved movement between farming areas, markets and homes even before work was complete. She said local leaders organised residents, including women, young people, widows and people with disabilities, to clear trees and other obstacles. Josephine said many women worked for three to four hours, but their payment was too little for the time and effort.

Ogenga said opening the road also gave people without jobs a chance to earn money. Josephine said the connection was especially important to farmers relying on produce from Palotaka, an area known for agricultural production.

ss.headline: Nuba Mountains education authorities report 3,728 pupils sat exams in South Sudan
ss.dek: The candidates took primary certificate examinations at nine centres in Ruweng, while insecurity kept 66 registered pupils away.
paragraphs: A total of 3,728 pupils from Sudan’s Nuba Mountains region sat primary school certificate examinations at nine centres in South Sudan’s Ruweng Administrative Area, regional education director-general Jamal Abdallah Kalo said. The exams ran from 16 to 20 November, with centres in Pariang and Yida.

Kalo said 3,794 pupils had registered, including 1,913 boys and 1,815 girls; 66 candidates were absent, among them 25 boys and 41 girls. He attributed the absences to insecurity in Heiban County, where schools remained closed amid displacement that began in May. Schools reopened for the first term on 1 October, but some in the region faced full or partial closures.

Secondary certificate exams for 1,213 registered students, from 15 schools across 14 counties, were scheduled to begin on 23 November. Kalo said shortages of school supplies and teaching materials, damaged in events in Kauda, and the closure of teacher training institutes were among the region’s education challenges.

ss.headline: University of Juba graduates more than 6,000 students
ss.dek: The 23-school class includes 1,503 master's graduates and 16 PhD holders, as officials urged them to serve South Sudan.
paragraphs: The University of Juba graduated more than 6,000 students from 23 schools on Saturday, 21 November, at its 28th convocation in South Sudan. President Salva Kiir Mayardit, the university's chancellor, presided over the ceremony.

Among the graduates are 1,325 diploma holders and 3,655 bachelor's degree recipients, alongside 277 postgraduate diploma holders, 1,503 master's graduates and 16 PhD holders. Vice Chancellor John Akech said some students had taken part-time jobs to pay tuition while facing financial difficulties and other challenges.

Caretaker General Education and Instruction Minister Kuyok Abol Kuyok urged graduates to contribute through service, innovation and leadership, saying families and communities had sacrificed to support their education. Government officials, university staff, students and parents attended.

ss.headline: Letter calls for citizens to control South Sudan dialogue agenda
ss.dek: The writer says a proposed Citizens’ Assembly needs independent conveners and representatives chosen by citizens, with leaders limited to presenting their views.
paragraphs: A letter published by Radio Tamazuj on Saturday calls for citizens to control the agenda of a proposed Citizens’ Assembly on South Sudan’s Future. The writer says the assembly needs independent conveners and citizens must be free to choose their representatives and raise their concerns.

The letter says political and military leaders may present their views, but the agenda should belong to citizens. It argues that people with greater power have greater duties, and calls on commanders in government and opposition to end attacks on civilians, open roads and allow aid through.
The writer also points to a 10 November 2026 call by the UN Mission in South Sudan for civilian protection and humanitarian access, saying people must be able to participate safely.

ss.headline: Ugandan comedians urge South Sudanese performers to build comedy platforms
ss.dek: Patrick Salvador says local talent lacks places to perform, while Dr Hilary Okello urges comedians to collaborate and start small projects.
paragraphs: Ugandan comedians Patrick Salvador and Dr Hilary Okello urged South Sudanese performers to work together and create more opportunities for the country’s comedy industry, speaking on Eye Radio’s Rhumba Show. Salvador said South Sudan has talented comedians but too few platforms to perform, gain experience and reach wider audiences.

Salvador said Uganda’s comedy scene grew after organised competitions gave performers places to showcase their work. He cited a competition launched by MultiChoice in 2009 to find the country’s funniest comedian, saying it helped a new generation, including him, establish careers. Okello urged emerging South Sudanese comedians to organise, collaborate and start small projects rather than wait for a theatre or other platform.

Okello said government, companies and other potential backers were more likely to support creatives who showed commitment through their own initiatives. John Chirbek, founder and host of the ninth Beledna Talk Show, said the programme connects South Sudanese entertainers with regional artists and professional opportunities beyond the country.

sd.headline: Rebel forces push within about 40 kilometers of Sudan's Damazin
sd.dek: Allied fighters took the Bau locality headquarters and entered Madina 11, while some Damazin residents have begun leaving for safer areas.
paragraphs: On Thursday and Friday, fighters from the Rapid Support Forces and the SPLM-North took Bau, the administrative seat of Bau locality, and moved into Madina 11 in Geisan locality. Videos filmed by RSF fighters and verified by Sudan War Monitor show them outside the Bau headquarters building.

The army pulled back from Bau to Miganza, about 20 kilometers to the north, according to Sudan War Monitor, which said the Geisan advance has brought the fighting to within about 40 kilometers of Damazin. Some residents have begun leaving, and a resident, Elham Kamal, told Radio Tamazuj that others want to go but cannot afford to travel to safer areas.

Sennar state, to the east, has imposed a night curfew and restrictions on goods transport and hot-drink sales from 8 p.m. to 5 a.m., because of fears the fighting could spread there. Sennar's governor issued Emergency Order No. 6 of 2026 on Saturday.

sd.headline: Sudan's army faces accusations after drone hits school sheltering displaced people in W...
sd.dek: Kordofan Observatory says a drone struck the Musab bin Umair Western School in Ghubaysh, which was sheltering hundreds displaced by fighting around En Nuhud, killing 16.
paragraphs: A drone struck a displacement shelter in Ghubaysh, West Kordofan State, on Tuesday night, killing at least 16 internally displaced people and injuring 10 others, according to a statement from Kordofan Observatory reported by Radio Tamazuj. The observatory blamed the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), saying the drone was allegedly theirs.

The observatory said the drone hit Musab bin Umair Western School at about 8 p.m., and that the school was sheltering hundreds of people who had fled fighting around En Nuhud. Imad Abdel Hadi, executive director of Ghubaysh Locality, said the army had repeatedly used drone strikes against towns and populated areas, and that Ghubaysh had come under successive drone attacks for three consecutive days.

Mohamed Hamid, a Ghubaysh resident, said army drones had repeatedly struck markets, residential neighbourhoods and schools, and called on the army to respect the civilian status of such sites and take precautions to protect civilians during military operations.

sd.headline: Khatmiyya family appoints Ali al-Mirghani as spiritual leader
sd.dek: The decision settles succession at one of Sudan’s largest Sufi orders but leaves the Democratic Unionist Party leadership unresolved.
paragraphs: The family of late Sudanese religious and political leader Mohamed Osman al-Mirghani appointed his eldest son, Ali, as spiritual leader of the Khatmiyya Sufi order, settling succession at one of Sudan’s largest such orders. The family announced the decision on Friday.

Jaafar al-Sadiq, one of Ali’s brothers, said the siblings had agreed to support Ali’s leadership. In his first address, Ali urged followers to settle differences through dialogue, respect opposing views and reject division. He has lived in the United States since the mid-1990s.

Control of the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) remains unresolved between brothers Mohamed al-Hassan and Jaafar al-Sadiq. Their rivalry predates their father’s death; they also take opposing sides in Sudan’s war, which began in April 2023 between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.

tg.headline: Togo adopts 2027 budget with 921 milliards FCFA for creditors
tg.dek: The plan balances at 2 684,05 milliards FCFA, with borrowing covering a 239,9 milliards FCFA deficit and debt repayments.
paragraphs: Togo’s government adopted its proposed 2027 budget, setting state resources and spending at 2 684,05 milliards FCFA. The plan allocates 1 915 milliards FCFA to budget spending, including 644 milliards FCFA for capital expenditure and 1 271 milliards FCFA for ordinary expenses.

The proposal puts tax revenue at 1 425,6 milliards FCFA and the budget deficit at 239,9 milliards FCFA, equal to 12,5 % of spending. It says borrowing will cover the deficit. The government expects to raise 959,8 milliards FCFA in treasury resources, including 371,8 milliards FCFA from public securities and 290,9 milliards FCFA in project loans.

Debt interest is set at 201,5 milliards FCFA, while loan repayments total 719,9 milliards FCFA. Together, those payments send 921 milliards FCFA to creditors, equivalent to 65 % of expected tax revenue. The budget bill was signed in Lomé on 22 October 2026.

tg.headline: Kara University project delivers three prototypes for rural farmers
tg.dek: Minodu developed irrigation, biopesticide and offline communication tools with communities in three localities over three years.
paragraphs: A three-year project at the University of Kara in Togo has developed three agricultural prototypes with rural communities, and ended on Friday, 20 November 2026. The work was carried out with the German Research Centre for Artificial Intelligence (DFKI), a German research institute, and began on 26 July 2023.

The prototypes include an irrigation device to manage water during irregular rainfall, a method for producing and using biopesticides against pests, and a digital community network that works without electricity or an internet connection. The network was installed in Tchitchao, Lama-Saoudè and Somdina-Haut, where it reaches users within a radius of 30 to 50 metres.

Project coordinator Professor Mikémina Pilo said students also received hybrid training with Berlin University of the Arts in designing and prototyping solutions. The project sought to connect university research with farmers’ needs, including low yields and limited access to scientific information.

tn.headline: Tunisia says alternative sentences exclude crimes
tn.dek: Justice Minister Leïla Jaffel told Parliament the measures apply only to eligible offences and require the convicted person’s consent.
paragraphs: Tunisia’s Justice Minister, Leïla Jaffel, told Parliament on Saturday that alternatives to prison do not apply to crimes and are limited to offences that meet legal conditions. She said the convicted person’s consent is one of the criteria.

Jaffel gave the figures during a joint plenary session on prisons and release mechanisms. Between 1 January and 17 November 2026, judges responsible for enforcing sentences granted conditional release to 3 423 detainees. A total of 10 363 detainees were released during that period, she said.

tn.headline: Greenpeace urges Tunisia to enforce plastic-bag restrictions
tn.dek: The group estimates plastic pollution costs Tunisia between $170 and $560 million a year and says the restrictions have been applied unevenly.
paragraphs: Greenpeace Middle East and North Africa urged Tunisia to strengthen enforcement of restrictions on some single-use plastic bags, which have been in force since January 2020. The organisation said the products remain in distribution channels despite the rules.

A Greenpeace report, The Hidden Price of Plastic, estimates annual costs linked to plastic pollution in Tunisia at between $170 and $560 million. The figures come from economic modelling, not recorded public spending. On nine beaches, 77% of the 9821 items collected were plastic, and 98.2% of waste with an identified origin came from Tunisia.

The report says banning some single-use plastic products could reduce plastic entering the Mediterranean by 23%. It also recommends extending producer responsibility to abandoned or lost fishing equipment, which made up 22.2% of the weight of waste observed on the beaches.

tn.headline: Tunisia reviews appointments for vacant mosque posts
tn.dek: Religious Affairs Minister Ahmed Bouhali says candidates are assessed by regional commissions as his department works to shorten delays.
paragraphs: Tunisia has 20 628 religious officials across 11 functions, Religious Affairs Minister Ahmed Bouhali told lawmakers during a joint session on his department’s 2027 budget. He outlined measures to fill vacant posts in mosques, speed up appointments and improve officials’ professional and social conditions.

Bouhali said officials are not assigned automatically to mosques with vacancies. Residents of the localities concerned propose candidates, who must complete administrative procedures and meet requirements including scientific and physical aptitude and commitment to Islamic values. A regional commission assesses each candidate’s skills and ability to perform the religious role.

Asked about delays between applications and appointment decisions, Bouhali said administrative procedures take time. He said the ministry is working to process applications faster to meet places of worship’s needs and maintain religious activities.

tn.headline: Tunisia tourism executive Adel Boussarsar dies
tn.dek: The former head of Tunisie Voyages and founder of Golden Yasmine Hotels worked in Tunisian tourism from the 1970s through 2016.
paragraphs: Adel Boussarsar, a Tunisian tourism executive who led Tunisie Voyages and developed the Golden Yasmine Hotels chain, died on Saturday, 21 November 2026, La Presse de Tunisie reported. He began working in tourism administration in 1971 and opened the Tunisian National Tourism Office's Paris representation in 1974.

Boussarsar took charge of Tunisie Voyages in 1984 and became the general agent in Tunisia of Germany's TUI, one of Europe's largest travel groups, on 31 December that year. The company managed transfers and excursions for TUI clients in Tunisia. His hotel chain operated properties in Hammamet, Tabarka, Kairouan, Tozeur and Douz; in March 2014, he announced the sale of eight hotel units.

He chaired Tunisia's travel-agencies federation until February 2006 and partly withdrew from Tunisie Voyages' operational management in 2011, while remaining board chairman. In 2003, Germany awarded him the Officer's Cross of the Order of Merit.

zm.headline: Standard & Poor's raises Zambia's sovereign rating to B-
zm.dek: The upgrade from CCC+/C carries a stable outlook, with the ratings agency citing debt-restructuring progress and sustained fiscal reforms.
paragraphs: S&P Global Ratings, the New York-based credit rating agency, raised Zambia's sovereign credit rating from CCC+/C to B-/B on November 20, 2026, and assigned a stable outlook. The move comes as the country's debt restructuring nears completion.

S&P cited improved economic performance, progress in restructuring debt and sustained fiscal reforms as reasons for the upgrade. Situmbeko Musokotwane, Zambia's finance and national planning minister, described it as an important milestone in the country's economic recovery.
The revised rating replaces the previous CCC+/C assessment; the announcement gave no further details on the restructuring's completion.

eh.headline: UN mission to leave Western Sahara by 31 January without holding referendum
eh.dek: MINURSO spent 35 years without organising the vote, while helping monitor the 1991 ceasefire between Morocco and the Polisario Front.
paragraphs: The United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) is due to leave the territory by 31 January 2027 without organising the self-determination referendum in its mandate, ECS Saharaui reported. The mission was created 35 years ago to let Sahrawis decide the territory's political future.

The referendum process stalled over disputes including the voter census and identification. Morocco opposed repeated efforts to update the census drawn up during Spanish rule, the report said. MINURSO also monitored the 1991 ceasefire between Morocco and the Polisario Front for decades.

Hostilities resumed in November 2020 after a Moroccan military intervention in the El Guerguerat area. Spanish journalist Ignacio Cembrero, who has followed the conflict for four decades, told RFI he fears a military escalation once the mission is gone.

eh.headline: Russia vetoes US Western Sahara resolution at UN Security Council
eh.dek: The US-backed draft would have renewed the United Nations Western Sahara mission to October 2027 and put Morocco's autonomy proposal at the centre of talks.
paragraphs: Russia vetoed a US draft resolution on Western Sahara at the UN Security Council on 30 October, blocking a proposed renewal of the UN peacekeeping mission in the territory, known as MINURSO (the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara). The text had support from 11 council members and would have extended the mission's mandate until October 2027.

The draft also proposed changing the mission's name and direction, with Morocco's autonomy plan at the centre of the political process. Russia said the text did not reflect the parties' positions and departed from the basis of negotiations, according to ECS Saharaui, a Spanish-language outlet covering the territory.
A Russian alternative to extend the mission also failed after the United States vetoed it, leaving the mission's renewal unresolved.

eh.headline: Former Algerian envoy warns Morocco could seize Polisario-held land after UN mission exits
eh.dek: Ammar Belani says Rabat could use the scheduled departure of the UN mission on 31 January 2027 to extend its control across the separation wall.
paragraphs: Ammar Belani, a former Algerian ambassador, has warned that Morocco may use the scheduled departure of the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) on 31 January 2027 to extend its occupation to the rest of the territory. He said the operation would aim to cross the separation wall and take the 20% of Western Sahara that the Polisario Front controls.

Belani said such an offensive could spread hostilities and raise the risk of a wider regional conflict. He also said Rabat would seek to sideline the Polisario Front through talks with Sahrawi groups that back Moroccan positions, including the Sahrawi Movement for Peace and former dissidents of the Sahrawi movement.

Belani added that Morocco would then propose an autonomy framework under its sovereignty, put to a constitutional consultation in Morocco and occupied Western Sahara. He said Rabat would seek support from the United States, France and Gulf states, and aim to have Western Sahara removed from the UN list of non-self-governing territories.

ls.headline: Lesotho authority trains local teams as it develops national cyber response
ls.dek: The interim response team is running a three-day programme after years of reliance on international specialists, the authority’s chief executive said.
paragraphs: Lesotho’s communications regulator is using a three-day cybersecurity training programme to build local capacity, as its interim response team works to strengthen the country’s ability to handle digital threats. The National Cybersecurity Capacity Building Week began at Mpilo Boutique Hotel and brings together local and international experts.

Authority chief executive Nizam Goolam said Lesotho had relied on international specialists for years and that the programme was intended to develop local expertise. The authority invited experts from the Cyber Capacity Centre for Southern Africa to help train Basotho. Cybersecurity manager Tumane Mahloane said the interim team, first established within the regulator under the Communications Act of 2012, now serves as the country’s interim computer emergency response team.

The government is working to establish a permanent national cybersecurity body. The week also included a two-day hackathon in which students from four universities and colleges competed to develop cybersecurity solutions; winners were due to be announced on Friday.
